item.title: Turning an image sequence into a video
item.content:
You'll render an animation from Blender as a folder of numbered PNG images, one per frame, and then turn them into a video: set the footage to the animation's frame rate in After Effects, and export an H.264 MP4 with Media Encoder. You'll need an animation in Blender (the video uses a stylized waterfall, 250 frames at 24 fps), After Effects and Media Encoder. The video uses Blender 4.2 and After Effects 2025, so some menus may look a little different in newer versions.

Render an image sequence in Blender

  1. Check the animation. 0:05 Play it back to see what you're rendering: here a stylized waterfall that runs for 250 frames. In the Output Properties, Frame Rate is 24 fps and the frame range is 1 to 250.

  2. Choose a folder for the images. 0:16 In the Output Properties, under Output, click the folder icon. In Blender's file browser, make a new folder for the images (here waterfall-images) 0:26, open it and click Accept 0:36.

  3. Save the frames as PNG. 0:38 Under Output, set File Format to PNG.

  4. Render the animation. 0:45 Choose Render → Render Animation. Blender renders each frame of the animation in turn and saves it into the folder 0:50.

Make it a video in After Effects

  1. Import the folder. 1:03 The folder now holds the numbered frames, 0001.png to 0250.png 1:05. Drag the folder into After Effects' Project panel 1:08: the images come in as one piece of footage, a PNG sequence named [0001-0250].png.

  2. Set the footage to 24 fps. 1:17 After Effects reads the sequence at 30 frames per second, which is wrong: the animation was made at 24. Right-click the footage, choose Interpret Footage → Main, set Assume this frame rate to 24 and click OK 1:24.

  3. Make a composition and preview it. 1:29 Drag the footage down into the empty timeline: After Effects makes a composition from it 1:31. Press Space to preview it 1:33. It should last roughly 10 seconds 1:36.

  4. Send it to Media Encoder. 1:43 Choose File → Export → Add to Adobe Media Encoder Queue. Media Encoder opens with the composition in its queue 1:49.

Export an H.264 video with Media Encoder

  1. Use H.264 with the Vimeo preset. 1:49 Here the composition comes in with the format H.264 and the preset Vimeo 1080p Full HD; keep them. If yours has another preset, click the Preset drop-down and select Vimeo 1080p Full HD 1:57. HEVC (H.265) is a newer standard you could use, but with it you lose the Vimeo preset 2:03, so the video goes back to H.264 and selects Vimeo 1080p Full HD again 2:12.

  2. Choose where the video goes. 2:21 Click the path under Output File. In the Save As dialog, choose a folder: here a new folder, waterfall-video, beside the folder of images 2:36. Then click Save 2:43.

  3. Start the queue. 2:46 Click the green play button at the top right of the queue. Media Encoder encodes the animation into the video file; here it takes about 20 seconds.

  4. Check the video. 3:00 When it's done, click the output file's path to show it in the Finder, and open the video (here Comp.mp4) to preview it 3:04.

Wrap-up

You've rendered a Blender animation as a sequence of PNG images, set the footage to its real frame rate in After Effects with Interpret Footage, and exported it from Media Encoder as an H.264 MP4 with the Vimeo 1080p Full HD preset.

From speech to text.
